## SCENE ONE: THE SIGNAL THAT DIDN'T ARRIVE

The orbital array had been transmitting for fourteen years.

Not continuously — the array cycled through its broadcast schedule with the precision of any well-designed system that had learned, through hard experience, to preserve power for the moments when power mattered most. Six hours of active transmission, eighteen hours of standby. A heartbeat. Regular, purposeful, patient.

It had broadcast on every frequency the mission's communications array could produce: high-band X-band for point-to-point, lower-frequency S-band for broader coverage, and the old VHF backup channel that nobody used anymore but that was kept active because it had once been the difference between rescue and catastrophe in a story everyone had heard and no one wanted to repeat.

The signal had been traveling toward Earth at the speed of light for fourteen years. That meant the people who had first heard it were fourteen years younger. That meant children who had been conceived after the colonists left were now old enough to understand the mathematics of distance. That meant the entire message had been received multiple times, analyzed by teams of specialists who would have spent their careers parsing every syllable for meaning, for tone, for the kind of subtext that people send across interplanetary distances whether they intend to or not.

What no one in the Mars First colony knew — what they had been trying not to think about since the fire, and before the fire, and in the long months between the fire and the decision that had sent them all the way across the solar system in the first place — was whether Earth was sending anything back anymore.

Arun found out on a Tuesday, which was an Earth concept that had survived in the colony's scheduling system purely because the human brain needed some way to mark the passage of time that wasn't just counting days.

He was in the communications bay, running a routine diagnostic on the primary receiver array after the fire had forced an emergency shutdown of all non-critical systems. The diagnostic was supposed to take forty minutes. It took sixty-three because three of the receiver's subsystems had been corrupted by what Arun suspected was a power surge during the fire's approach, and corrupted subsystems on Mars were not something you replaced, they were something you rebuilt from scratch using parts that were meant for different equipment entirely.

He was elbow-deep in a diagnostic readout, comparing nominal values against current readings and trying to decide which discrepancies were fixable and which were going to require cannibalizing something else, when the receiver flagged an anomalous signal.

Not a response. Not a message. An absence.

Arun noticed it the way a musician notices a missing note — not because something was there, but because something was not. The receiver had been picking up, for years, a background hum across multiple frequencies. It was not a transmission, exactly. It was more like the electromagnetic signature of a planet that was active, industrial, alive. The kind of signal you get from an Earth that is still transmitting across all the frequencies it has always transmitted on: weather satellites, military communications, deep space network, commercial broadcasting, navigation systems, the ceaseless electromagnetic chatter of a civilization that has never stopped talking to itself.

The absence was in one specific frequency band — a band that had been occupied, during the last routine check sixty-two days before the fire, by a repeating automated signal from the European Space Agency's Mars relay satellite.

That signal was not there anymore.

Arun ran a diagnostic. Checked the receiver's calibration. Verified that the antenna was pointed at the correct coordinates. The receiver was fine. The antenna was fine. The pointing was correct.

The signal simply wasn't there.

He moved to the next band. The one carrying Chinese deep space network traffic. Gone.

He moved to the next. NASA's Deep Space Network carrier signal. The one that had been as constant as a lighthouse since the colony's arrival, the steady heartbeat of communication with mission control in Houston, which had been, for fifteen years, as reliable as gravity.

Also gone.

Arun sat back in his chair and stared at the diagnostic screen until the cursor blinked itself into a pattern that suggested, if you were in the right frame of mind, a flat line.

His first instinct — the instinct of an engineer who has spent his career solving problems that have solutions — was to assume equipment failure. The receiver, the antenna, the power supply, the signal processing board, any one of a dozen components that could have failed and produced exactly this result.

He ran another diagnostic. This one took longer because he was running it the way you run diagnostics when you already know what you're going to find and you are giving yourself as much time as possible to prepare for finding it.

The equipment was fine. The receiver was picking up signals from other sources — cosmic background radiation, solar wind interference, the faint electromagnetic signature of Jupiter's magnetosphere, all the usual noise. But from Earth, on the frequencies where there had always been continuous presence: nothing.

He tried the emergency frequency. The one that was supposed to be monitored twenty-four hours a day, three hundred and sixty-five days a year, the frequency that existed specifically for situations exactly like the one he was beginning to suspect he was in.

Nothing. Not silence — silence is an absence of sound. This was something worse: the absence of presence. The kind of absence that only becomes visible when you've become so accustomed to presence that you've stopped noticing it.

Arun leaned back. He was a man who had spent his career building systems that worked under conditions that nobody believed were possible, a man who had designed and implemented the power grid of a Mars colony and had kept it running through dust storms and equipment failures and now fire, a man who had learned, through fifteen years of problem-solving, that there was always a solution if you looked hard enough and long enough and from enough different angles.

He could not find a solution for this. Because this was not a technical problem. It was, at best, a technical symptom of something that was happening on a world twelve light-minutes away and that he had no way of understanding or influencing or even fully comprehending.

Because the question was not whether the receiver was broken.

The question was whether anyone on the other end was still transmitting.

## SCENE TWO: THE WEIGHT OF DISCOVERY

Arun took his findings to Elena. Not because he wanted to share the burden — although he did — but because he had learned, in fifteen years of working alongside the woman who had been the mission's chief engineer and was now, effectively, its de facto leader, that Elena needed to know everything as soon as it became relevant, and this was relevant at a level that made almost everything else seem trivial.

He found her in the agricultural wing, which was still recovering from the fire's indirect effects — not the direct damage, which had been contained, but the secondary effects of smoke infiltration on the plant systems, the kind of damage that couldn't be seen immediately and that revealed itself slowly, over days, as plants that had seemed fine began to yellow and wither and fail.

Elena was on her knees beside one of the affected hydroponic beds, her hands deep in the nutrient solution, examining roots with the careful attention of someone who had learned that the difference between life and death in a closed ecosystem was often measured in millimeters of root growth.

"Arun," she said without looking up. "Tell me it's not the power grid."

"It's not the power grid."

"Good. Because if it's the power grid, I'm going to —" She pulled her hands from the nutrient solution and stood, wiping them on her coveralls, and then she saw his face.

She stopped. Because Arun was not a man who came to people with the expression he was wearing right now unless the thing he was bringing was something that needed immediate attention. His face was a careful construction of professional neutrality, but there was something underneath it that Elena had learned to recognize over fifteen years of working together.

It was the face he wore when he had found a problem that he didn't think he could solve.

"Come with me," he said. "Comms bay."

They walked in silence. That, too, was unusual. Arun was a man who filled silence with data, with explanation, with the kind of continuous stream of technical information that made people around him feel informed and grounded. His silence meant that there were no words for what he had found, or that the words he had were not the kind of words he wanted to say.

In the comms bay, Arun pulled up the diagnostic on the main screen. He didn't explain immediately. He let the data speak first, the way he always did — because data, unlike interpretation, did not carry the weight of the person presenting it, and sometimes the person receiving it needed to encounter the information before encountering the interpretation.

Elena looked at the screen. Then she looked at Arun.

"Run the test again."

"I've run it four times."

"Run it a fifth time."

He ran it a fifth time. The results were identical.

Elena stood in front of the screen for a long time. The screen showed, in the most neutral possible way, the absence of communication from Earth. Not intermittent. Not degraded. Absent.

She thought about the last transmission she had received from mission control. It had been seventy-one days ago — before the fire, during one of the routine scheduled communication windows. The content had been standard: status requests, supply chain updates, a brief personal message from someone at NASA who had been with the mission since the beginning. Nothing to suggest that anything was wrong. Nothing to suggest that the person sending it might not be there to send another one.

"When did you first notice?" Elena asked.

"During the post-fire diagnostic. I was checking the receiver array and realized the carrier signals from the primary Earth transmission bands were absent. At first I thought it was equipment failure — receiver damage, antenna misalignment, something local. I ran full diagnostics. The equipment is fine. The signals are simply not there."

"All of them?"

"All the ones I've been able to check. ESA Mars relay, NASA DSN, Chinese deep space network. On all the standard frequencies, nothing."

Elena turned away from the screen. She walked to the nearest wall and leaned against it, which was something Arun had never seen her do. Elena was not a wall-leaner. She was a face-the-problem-head-on, arms-crossed, chin-squared person. Wall-leaning meant that the problem was too large to face directly.

"How long?" she asked.

"Without continuous monitoring, I can't say. The last confirmed Earth signal reception was sixty-two days ago, before the fire. The fire forced us to shut down the receiver for emergency power conservation. We only brought it back online yesterday. So the absence could be anywhere from a few days to two months. Or longer."

"Or longer," Elena repeated.

Arun nodded.

Elena closed her eyes. When she opened them, they were the eyes of someone who was already calculating, already working through the implications, already building a mental model of the situation that would allow her to make decisions.

"We need to tell the council," she said.

"The full council?"

"The full council. This is not something we can contain to a smaller group."

Arun nodded again. He had known this would be her answer. He had also known that she would ask him to run the test again anyway, because Elena was thorough, and thoroughness in the face of catastrophe was both a virtue and a form of self-preservation — the need to be absolutely certain before accepting that the worst had happened.

## SCENE THREE: THE COUNCIL

There were twelve people on the Mars First council, representing the various functional divisions of the colony: engineering, life support, agriculture, medicine, science, communications, security, logistics, administration, education, construction, and — informally, because it had proved impossible to exclude her — the medical lead, Laila.

They gathered in the common area, the room that had once been designed for community dinners and movie nights and the kind of social interaction that made a group of two hundred people feel connected to each other. The fire had not damaged this room, but the atmosphere of the colony had, and the room felt different now — smaller, somehow, or heavier, as if the air itself was aware of the things they were gathering to discuss.

Elena stood at the front of the room. She did not use the screen. She did not need to — the message was too simple for screens.

"We have lost communication with Earth," she said.

The silence that followed was not the same silence that had filled the colony after the birth. That silence had been awe — the silence of people recognizing that something extraordinary had happened. This silence was fear — the silence of people recognizing that something extraordinary had happened and that it was the wrong kind of extraordinary.

Laila, sitting in the back row, closed her eyes briefly. She had just delivered the first human being born on Mars three days ago, and she had not had time to process the enormity of that before being confronted with the enormity of this.

"What does that mean?" asked Marcus, the logistics lead. It was the kind of question people ask when they are hoping the answer will be simple and know, in their heart, that it will not be.

"It means," Elena said carefully, "that we are not receiving any signals from Earth on the frequencies we have always received them on. This could mean several things. It could mean a transient failure on Earth's transmission infrastructure — a solar event, a terrestrial crisis, something temporary. It could mean an equipment failure at our end that my diagnostics have not detected. Or it could mean that Earth is no longer transmitting at all."

Marcus's face went pale. "No Fleet Coming," he said, and the words came out not as a question but as a statement, the kind of statement that people make when they are naming something they have been trying not to think about.

"No Fleet Coming," Elena confirmed.

The phrase had been in the mission's contingency planning from the beginning. It was the scenario everyone hoped would never need to be addressed, the scenario that was included in the documentation because any responsible organization had to plan for all possibilities, including the most terrible ones.

NO FLEET COMING: Protocol for sustained loss of contact with Earth in which no resupply, reinforcement, or extraction is anticipated. Assumes permanent or indefinite severing of Earth-Mars communication. Assumes that the colony must function as a self-contained and self-sustaining entity. All prior assumptions regarding supply chain, personnel rotation, and technological support from Earth are null and void.

The protocol existed. It had existed since before the colony arrived, since before the first ship landed, since the day that two hundred people had committed themselves to a planet that might kill them and an Earth that might forget them.

Nobody had ever wanted to read it aloud. Nobody had ever wanted to activate it. It was the protocol that existed only in theory, the plan for a scenario so extreme that acknowledging it felt like tempting fate.

Now it was not theoretical anymore.

"What are our numbers?" asked someone from the back — Dinesh, agriculture, his hands covered with the faint green marks that plant nutrient solution left on skin.

Elena had the numbers. Of course she had the numbers. She had always had the numbers, because having the numbers was how she coped with situations that were otherwise too large to process.

"Current supplies: forty-seven days of food at full ration, sixty-eight days at reduced ration. Water recycling at ninety-two percent efficiency — we are losing eight percent per cycle through system degradation. Oxygen production at eighty-four percent of nominal — the algae bioreactors took a hit from the power fluctuations during the fire. Medical supplies: adequate for routine care, limited for major emergencies. Replacement parts: sufficient for approximately eighteen months of maintenance, assuming no catastrophic failures."

A pause.

"Consumables: six months of air filter replacements, four months of sealant, three months of specialty lubricants. After that, we are improvising."

Another pause. Elena let the numbers settle in the room. Numbers were hard. Numbers did not lie. Numbers told you exactly where you stood, which was both their mercy and their cruelty.

"The bottom line," Elena continued, "is that we are self-sufficient for approximately three months at current consumption levels. After that, we are dependent on our ability to produce everything we need from local resources. Which we are already doing — partially. The agriculture wing is producing approximately forty percent of our caloric needs. The water recycling system is functioning within acceptable parameters. The oxygen production system needs rebuilding, which is a priority."

She looked around the room at the faces of the people she had worked with for fifteen years. They were tired. They were damaged. They were scared. And they were listening.

"This means that every decision we make from this point forward has different weight," she said. "Decisions that were reversible when Earth was a phone call away are irreversible now. Decisions that were low-stakes are high-stakes. Decisions that we could defer are decisions we must make."

She paused again. Let that sink in.

"I know what you're thinking," she said. "You're thinking: did everyone on Earth—? You're thinking: is there a war? A pandemic? A catastrophe? You're thinking about your families, your children, your parents, your friends, and you are wondering whether they are safe, and we cannot answer that question. We cannot answer any question about Earth, because Earth is not answering."

The room was so quiet that the hum of the ventilation system — the system that Arun had repaired after the fire, the system that pumped air through the habitat and kept them alive — sounded like a voice.

"But here is what we can say," Elena continued, and her voice had shifted, found a register that was deeper and steadier than it had been a minute ago. "Here is what we can say with absolute certainty: we are alive. We are here. Mars is not going anywhere. We built this colony. We maintained this colony. We survived the fire. We survived the birth. We will survive this."

She looked at each person in the room. One by one. Making eye contact. Not pleading. Not inspiring. Simply connecting, in the way that people who have shared fifteen years of the most difficult experience of their lives could connect across a room without speaking.

"The NO FLEET COMING protocol is now active," she said. "Effective immediately. All operations will be reoriented to permanent self-sufficiency. All resource allocation will reflect the understanding that Earth is not sending resupply. All planning will assume that we are — and will remain — the only humans on Mars for the foreseeable future."

She sat down. Nobody spoke. Nobody moved.

Then Laila stood.

## SCENE FOUR: WHAT COMES AFTER THE END OF HOPE

Laila did not usually speak at council meetings. Her domain was medical — the human body, the systems that kept it functioning, the things that could go wrong and the things that could be done about them. She left the politics to people who had the temperament for it, and temperament was not something Laila had ever claimed to possess in abundance.

But she was standing now, and the room turned to her with the kind of attention that people pay when the person who rarely speaks stands up.

Laila walked to the front of the room. She did not stand at a podium or use a screen. She simply stood, hands at her sides, and addressed two hundred colleagues who were waiting, for the first time in fifteen years, to hear words that would not be followed by a plan from Earth.

"I just want to say one thing," she said.

Her voice was not what people expected. It was not the commanding, authoritative voice she used in the medbay during emergencies. It was quieter. Softer. Almost — the word would not have occurred to anyone who knew Laila — gentle.

"Three days ago," Laila said, "Sana and Tariq's child was born. The first human being born on Mars. I delivered him."

She paused. Her eyes did not move around the room. They stayed fixed on a point in the distance, as if she were looking at something that only she could see.

"When I held him, the first thing I noticed was his hands. They were very small. Very fragile. Everything about him was fragile — the way newborns are, the way all human beings are at the beginning, when they have not yet been shaped by the world they have entered. His skin was pink. His cry was strong. He was, by every measure I have, a healthy child."

She turned her eyes back to the room.

"That child has never seen Earth. He will never see Earth. The planet he was born on, the planet he is adapted to, the planet that will shape his body and his mind and his understanding of the world is this one. Mars. This dusty, difficult, unforgiving place that we have been trying to survive on for fifteen years."

Her voice did not rise. It did not change its steady, measured cadence. But the effect it had on the room was profound, the way that a single note, played with sufficient conviction, can change the quality of an entire piece of music.

"I am telling you this because I think it matters. Not in the way that supply chains and oxygen production and resource allocation matter — though those things do matter, and I am not saying they don't. I am telling you this because the birth of a child on Mars means something specific, and that meaning is: we are not temporary."

She let that hang for a moment.

"We came here on fifteen-year contracts. We came here assuming that we would eventually go home. We came here with return tickets packed in the back of our minds, with the assumption that Earth would always be there to catch us, to resupply us, to remind us that we were part of something larger than ourselves. And maybe Earth still is. Maybe everyone on Earth is fine and there is a technical explanation for the lost signals and the comms will come back online next week and this will all seem like a momentary panic."

She paused.

"But maybe not. And if not, we need to understand what that means. It means that the child I delivered three days ago is not just a child. He is a statement. He is us saying, without using words that anyone on Earth can hear, that we are staying. That this is not a mission anymore. That it has been a home for a long time and we just didn't want to admit it."

Marcus, the logistics lead, had raised his hand. Laila nodded at him.

"Laila," he said, his voice tight. "I have two daughters. In Seattle. I haven't seen them in fifteen years. If Earth is gone—"

"I know," Laila said. The words were not a dismissal. They were an acknowledgment, the kind of acknowledgment that can only come from someone who has spent her career sitting with people in their worst moments and learning that the right thing to do is not always to offer hope but sometimes to sit with the absence of it.

"If Earth is gone, your daughters are on Earth," she said. "And Earth is a big planet. It has survived everything we have thrown at it for four billion years. If anyone can survive whatever is happening, they can. They are on the most resilient planet in the solar system. And we are on the second most resilient."

She looked at Marcus directly.

"You did a good thing for them, Marcus. You came here to build something that would outlast all of us. You didn't just come to visit Mars. You came to make it matter. And your daughters — wherever they are, whatever they are doing — are part of the reason this colony exists. Every decision you make now, every hour you put into keeping this place running, is for them. Not so you can go back. But so that the place you built for them has meaning."

Marcus put his head in his hands. The people around him did not say anything. They did not need to. The silence was sufficient — the silence of people who had made similar choices, for similar reasons, and who were sitting in the aftermath of discovering that the world they had left behind might no longer be the world they left.

Elena stood up after Laila sat down. The two women did not need to coordinate — they had never needed to coordinate, because their thinking aligned in the way that thinking aligns when two people have been forced, by circumstance and necessity and the accumulated weight of shared experience, to see the world in essentially the same way.

"We will make a decision in forty-eight hours," Elena said. "Forty-eight hours to process. Forty-eight hours to talk to our people, to our teams, to the colony. Forty-eight hours to decide whether we are declaring Mars First a permanent settlement or a temporary one. I know what I believe the answer is. I know what the data says the answer should be. But this is not a decision I will make alone."

She looked around the room.

"For forty-eight hours, we keep working. We keep the lights on. We keep the air moving. We keep the food growing. And we keep the children safe — all the children, starting with the one who was born three days ago and who is, whether we are ready for it or not, the reason we are having this conversation."

The meeting ended. The council dispersed. The people of Mars First returned to their posts and their stations and the endless, unglamorous work of keeping two hundred humans alive on a world that had never asked for them and would never stop trying, in subtle and not-so-subtle ways, to remind them that they did not belong.

But they were starting to understand, in the way that understanding comes not from a single revelation but from the accumulation of experiences that point in the same direction, that belonging was not something that was given. It was something that was earned.

And they had been earning it for fifteen years.

## SCENE FIVE: THE LONGEST NIGHT

Elena could not sleep.

She sat in the dim light of her quarters, the room she had occupied for fifteen years and that contained, with brutal efficiency, the sum total of her material existence: a bed, a desk, a chair, a shelf with seventeen books that were mostly technical manuals, a photo of her parents that had been printed on the first day of the mission and had faded from exposure to the colony's harsh lighting, and a small, battered model of the first Mars lander that a technician had built for her out of scrap parts during a particularly difficult phase of habitat construction.

She held the model in her hands. It was crude — the parts had not been designed for this purpose, and the result was something that looked more like an abstract sculpture than a lander — but it was hers, and the act of holding it was the act of holding onto something that connected her to the person she had been fifteen years ago, the person who had boarded a ship with the expectation of returning, of completing a mission, of going home.

That person was gone. Not dead — changed. Changed in the way that people change when they encounter things that cannot be unencountered, when they cross thresholds that cannot be uncrossed, when they wake up one morning and realize that the life they have been living is not the life they thought they were living.

She thought about Earth. Not about specific places — she had done that already, in the first years, in the dark nights when sleep wouldn't come and the mind wandered to coastlines and mountain ranges and cities and rivers and the kind of geography that feels impossibly vivid when you are trapped inside a metal structure surrounded by red rock and thin air. She thought about it in the abstract now: the planet itself, the blue marble, the thing that she and everyone in this colony had left behind with the assumption that it would always be there.

What if it wasn't?

Not gone — that was too dramatic, too final. What if it was changed? What if the Earth they had left was no longer the Earth that existed? What if the signals had been lost not because the transmitters had failed but because there was no one left to send them?

She couldn't know. She would probably never know. And the not-knowing was its own kind of grief — not the clean grief of loss, which at least has a shape and a direction, but the murky, shapeless grief of uncertainty, of wondering and never knowing and never being able to stop wondering.

A knock on the door. Two precise raps. Arun's knock.

"Come in," she called, setting the model down.

Arun entered. He was holding two cups of the colony's version of coffee — a reconstituted beverage that bore only a theoretical relationship to the real thing but that served the essential purpose of being warm and slightly caffeinated and therefore a reasonable facsimile of comfort.

"I couldn't sleep," he said, handing her a cup.

"Neither could I."

He sat in the chair opposite her desk. They drank in silence for a while, the kind of silence that people who have worked together for fifteen years don't need to fill with words.

"I ran the diagnostics again," Arun said eventually. "Different angles, different approaches, tried every way I can think of to prove the receiver is wrong. It's not wrong. The signals are not there."

Elena nodded. "I know."

"I looked at the solar weather data. No significant solar events in the last two months. No coronal mass ejections large enough to disrupt Earth's transmission infrastructure. No solar flares that would have knocked out the transmitters. Whatever is happening, it isn't solar."

"So it's terrestrial," Elena said.

"Or it's us."

"It's not us. We've checked. I've checked. You've checked. The equipment is fine."

Arun was quiet. Then: "Elena. Do you think—?"

"I don't know what I think." The admission came out more easily than she expected. "I think there are possibilities. Solar event, terrestrial crisis, equipment cascade on Earth's end— the list is long and none of them can be confirmed. What I do know is that we cannot base our planning on speculation. We have to base it on what we can observe. And what we can observe is that the signals are gone."

"And what we can't observe is—" Arun stopped.

"What we can't observe is everyone we know," Elena finished. "Everyone we love. Everyone we left behind. The children who were babies when we left and are adults now. The parents who said goodbye and promised to wait. The friends who said they'd be here when we got back."

She set the cup down. She looked at Arun, really looked at him, in the way that people look at each other when the formalities have been exhausted and what remains is something rawer, more honest, and less comfortable.

"Arun. I need you to know something."

He looked back. His eyes were tired. Everyone's eyes were tired.

"We are going to be all right," Elena said. "Not because I can promise that no one will die. In a Mars colony, people die — we all know that, we've all accepted that, we made our peace with it before we stepped off the ship. But because the people in this colony are the best I have ever seen. They are engineers who can build anything from nothing. They are farmers who can grow food in red dust. They are medics who can deliver babies in burning buildings. They are the kind of human beings who, when faced with the impossible, don't ask whether it can be done — they ask how fast they can do it."

Arun smiled. It was a small smile, the kind of smile that people manage when they are not feeling particularly amused but want to show the person speaking that they are listening.

"That was supposed to be my speech," he said.

"I got to it first."

They sat in quiet for a while. The ventilation system hummed. Somewhere in the distance, a baby cried — not Sana and Tariq's baby, not tonight, but one of the colony's younger children who had woken from a bad dream and was being comforted by a tired parent in a small room three corridors away.

The sound of a child crying in the night. The most ordinary sound in the world. And the most extraordinary, because on Earth it was so common that nobody paid attention to it, and on Mars it was a reminder that the most human of human things was happening here, in this place, against every probability.

"Elena," Arun said, standing to leave. "When you said it — permanent settlement. Did you mean it?"

"I meant it."

"Even without Earth?"

"Especially without Earth," Elena said. "Earth was the thing keeping us in the mindset of visitors. Visitors don't invest the same way that residents do. Visitors think in terms of contracts and missions and return dates. Residents think in terms of generations. And we have a generation, Arun. We have a baby. We have the first of what might be many. That baby changes everything. It means we can't think of this as a mission anymore. It has to be something else. Something permanent. Something that lasts."

Arun nodded slowly. He looked at the door, then back at Elena.

"I believe you," he said. "I believe it can be permanent. I believe in the people here. I believe in Sana's baby. I believe that we can do this." He paused. "I just wish we didn't have to find out we had to do it by losing everyone else."

Elena stood. She walked to the door with him. Before he left, she put a hand on his shoulder — the kind of gesture that was almost alien on Elena, who was not physically affectionate, who expressed care through competence rather than touch.

"We didn't lose them," she said. "We haven't confirmed that. And even if we have, even in the absolute worst case, the reason they're gone doesn't make what we built meaningless. We built it because they believed in it. Because they sent us here to do it. Whatever happens, that doesn't change."

Arun looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded, once, and left.

Elena closed the door. She stood in the dim light of her quarters, surrounded by the seventeen books and the faded photograph and the crude model of the first lander, and she felt, for the first time in a very long time, something that was not fear and not grief and not the weight of responsibility that had been her constant companion since the day she arrived on Mars.

She felt determination.

The kind of determination that comes not from hope but from something deeper — the decision, made at a level below consciousness, that the work is not finished and that it will be finished not because the universe demands it but because the people doing it refuse to stop.

She sat down at her desk. She pulled up a blank document. She began writing.

MARS FIRST COLONY — PERMANENT SETTLEMENT DECLARATION
DRAFT — FOR COUNCIL REVIEW
DATE: [STATION TIME], SOL 5,487

TO THE MEMBERS OF THE MARS FIRST COLONY:

Effective immediately, and pending formal council ratification, Mars First Colony is transitioning from Mission Status to Permanent Settlement Status...

She wrote through the night. Through the darkness of a Martian desert that she could not see through the bulkhead walls but could feel, in the way that people who have lived in a place for a long time can feel the landscape pressing against the doors and windows, reminding them of its presence.

When the colony's artificial dawn came on the morning cycle — not dawn, of course, not real dawn, just the gradual brightening of the habitat's lights that simulated the passage of a sun that was, from this distance, no larger than a bright coin in the sky — Elena was still writing, the words flowing faster now, finding their own rhythm, building the framework for a new version of a community that had, for fifteen years, been defined by its relationship to a world it might never see again.

She finished as the colony woke. She saved the document. She sent it to the council members. And then she stood, stretched her stiff back, and walked out into the corridor to begin the day's work.

Because the colony needed her. The people needed her. The baby — the first baby, the proof that life could take root in the most improbable of places — needed her, not directly, not yet, but in the way that every child needs the adults around them to keep building the world the child will grow up in.

And Elena was, above all else, a builder.

She walked through the corridors of Habitat Three. Past the scorched walls that were still being repaired. Past the people who were already at work, already doing the things that needed doing. Past the medical bay where Laila was already awake, already checking on Sana and Tariq and their son, already making sure that the first human being born on Mars was starting his life in the safest hands the colony could offer.

At the junction between corridors C and D, she paused. On the wall, someone — she didn't know who, and it didn't matter who — had written something in permanent marker, the kind of message that people leave in places that matter:

WE ARE STILL HERE.

Elena looked at it. She touched it, her fingers brushing the uneven letters, and then she kept walking.

Because the fleet wasn't coming.

And they didn't need it to.
"}

## SCENE ONE: THE ROOM NOBODY WANTED

It started as a storage bay.

Not a storage bay in the way that most colonists understood storage bays — the small, windowless rooms scattered through the habitat's interior where spare parts and emergency supplies and the accumulated detritus of fifteen years of continuous habitation were stacked, catalogued, and occasionally retrieved when something broke and someone needed to find the three-millimeter washer that had been placed in Storage Bay Seven on Sol 1,203 and never moved since.

This was a different kind of storage bay. Larger, deeper, located at the far end of Habitat Three's western corridor where the ambient light was dimest and the sound of the ventilation system arrived as a distant whisper rather than a presence. Storage Bay 22-West. It had been used, over the years, for exactly one purpose: storing the bodies.

Not permanently. There had never been a plan for permanent body storage. The mission protocols had been clear on this point, as they were on most points that involved things that people didn't want to think about until they had to: any deaths during the mission would result in cryogenic preservation of the remains until a return vessel became available, at which point the deceased would be transported home. It was the kind of protocol that was both comforting and absurd — comforting because it acknowledged the humanity of the people who might die, absurd because it assumed that a return vessel would always be available and that the Earth these people had left behind would always be a place worth returning to.

There had been three deaths in fifteen years. Three. A number that, statistically, was both extraordinarily low and exactly what you would expect when a group of two hundred people spent fifteen years in the most carefully designed and meticulously maintained habitat ever constructed by human hands, staffed by professionals who were selected not just for their competence but for their physical and psychological resilience.

Three deaths. Not zero — zero was impossible, a statistical fantasy that no one who understood probability would ever propose. But three. The first had been on Sol 412, when a micrometeorite had punctured a pressure seal during a routine EVA. Chen Wei, a geologist from Beijing, had been the most experienced EVA technician in the mission, and the probability assessment had put the risk of his particular mission at less than one percent. He had died anyway, because probability is a statement about averages and individuals do not live in averages.

The second had been on Sol 2,187. Olena Kovalenko, a botanist from Kyiv, who had suffered a pulmonary embolism despite the colony's rigorous health monitoring and preventive medicine protocols. Laila had been with her when it happened, had tried everything she could try, had administered every medication available, and had watched the most skilled agricultural scientist in the colony die in twelve minutes from something that, on Earth, would have been diagnosed and treated in an emergency room in less than one.

The third had been on Sol 4,902, just eighteen months before the fire. Tariq's father — no, not Tariq's father. Tariq's father was alive, at least he had been, the last time the colony had received signals from Earth. The third death had been Priya Sharma, an engineer from Mumbai who had been conducting maintenance on the reactor's cooling system and had been caught in a steam release when a valve failed. She had been warned. The valve had been flagged as degraded. But the work had needed doing, and the colony had been short-handed, and Priya had been the best person for the job, and sometimes the best person for the job is the person who dies because the best person for the job was the only person for the job.

Three bodies. Preserved cryogenically in Storage Bay 22-West, in specialized containment units that were designed to keep the deceased at temperatures low enough to slow decomposition to a practical standstill, waiting for a return ship that had never come and now, with the communications blackout and the activation of the NO FLEET COMING protocol, would never come.

They were not bodies anymore, not really. Not in the way that people think of bodies when they use the word. They were frozen. They were suspended. They existed in a state that was neither alive nor fully dead, caught in the gap between the medical definition of death and the physical reality of a body that had not yet begun its final transformation.

But they were gone. Everyone in the colony understood this. Grief does not require a body to be warm — it requires a body to be absent, and absence was something the frozen containment units of Storage Bay 22-West provided in abundance.

For fifteen years, the room had been a room that no one entered unless they had to. The containment units were remotely monitored, the temperature data transmitted to Laila's medical console on a regular schedule, but no one had walked into Storage Bay 22-West and stood beside those units since the last one was placed there, eighteen months ago, by a group of people who had done their duty and then left and then tried very hard to think about other things.

Until now.

Until the realization that the return ship was never coming turned Storage Bay 22-West from a temporary holding facility into something else entirely — not something anyone wanted to name, because naming it meant accepting it, and accepting it meant acknowledging, in concrete and physical terms, what the NO FLEET COMING protocol had already made abstractly clear.

The dead were not going home.

And someone had to decide what that meant.

## SCENE TWO: THE DECISION

Elena found Laila in the medbay. She was always there — not literally, she slept and ate and lived like everyone else, but in the way that the heart is always in the chest, Laila was always in the medbay, the person whose presence was the defining feature of the room and whose absence, when it occurred, was immediately noticeable to everyone who entered.

Today she was not with a patient. She was sitting at her desk, the desk she had claimed in the original medbay and then rebuilt in the fire-damaged version, reviewing medical supply inventories with the kind of focused attention that she brought to every task, large or small, because for Laila every task was equally deserving of her complete engagement.

"Laila," Elena said.

Laila looked up. "Elena."

"I need to talk to you about something. It's not a medical emergency. But it's medical-adjacent."

Laila set down the inventory tablet. She did not ask what it was about immediately. Elena had learned, over fifteen years, that Laila's pauses were not deliberation — they were preparation, the brief mental process by which she arranged her attention so that when the information came, it would be received by someone who was fully present to receive it.

"Storage Bay 22-West," Elena said.

Laila's expression did not change. But Elena had been reading Laila's face for fifteen years, and she had learned to detect the changes that existed beneath the surface — the micro-contractions, the barely perceptible shifts in eye movement, the way Laila's breathing slowed when she encountered information that required emotional processing before intellectual processing could begin.

"We need to talk about the deceased," Elena continued. "About Chen, Olena, and Priya. About what happens to their remains. Because the return ship is not coming, Laila. It's not coming, and we both know it, and pretending otherwise is an exercise in denial that the colony cannot afford."

Laila was quiet for a long time. The kind of quiet that was not empty but full — full of memory, full of the faces of the three people she had lost, full of the specific and particular way each of them had died and the specific and particular way each of them had lived.

"I've been avoiding thinking about it," Laila said. The admission surprised them both. Laila did not admit to avoidance. She was the person who ran toward problems, not away from them. The idea of Laila avoiding anything was like the idea of water refusing to be wet — technically possible under certain exotic conditions but essentially a contradiction in terms.

"Me too," Elena said. Then: "We can't keep avoiding it. The containment units require power. Not a lot — the cryogenic systems are efficient by design — but some. And power is something we can't afford to waste on bodies that are not coming back to life."

"I know." Laila stood. She walked to the supply cabinet, opened it, and began checking inventory with the mechanical efficiency of someone whose hands needed something to do while her mind processed information that her emotions were not yet ready to handle. "Three containment units. Each drawing approximately fifty watts. One hundred fifty watts total. Over a year, that's—"

"I know the numbers, Laila. One hundred fifty watts over a year is a significant amount of power in a colony that is rationing everything. But this isn't about the numbers."

"What is it about, then?"

Elena sat down in the chair opposite Laila's desk. She leaned forward, her elbows on her knees, her hands clasped in front of her — a posture Laila had learned to recognize as the Elena equivalent of vulnerability.

"It's about how we decide to remember people," Elena said. "Right now, Chen and Olena and Priya are in a storage bay. A storage bay, Laila. Not a memorial. Not a place of remembrance. A room where we put things we need to keep but don't want to see. That's what it is. And I don't think that's what they deserve."

Laila stopped checking inventory. She turned slowly from the supply cabinet and looked at Elena.

"What do you suggest?"

Elena took a breath. "A memorial. A permanent one. A place in the colony where the deceased are not stored but honored. Where their names are visible, where their contributions are recorded, where the people who come after them — and there will be people who come after them, because Sana's baby is proof of that — will know that humans died on Mars and that they mattered."

Laila was silent for a long time. When she spoke, her voice was quieter than it usually was, the voice she used when she was talking not about a medical procedure or a supply inventory but about something that existed in the space between the physical world and the world of memory.

"It should be in Storage Bay 22-West," she said.

Elena looked up, surprised. "You think so?"

"I think it's the right room. It's the room that has held them for fifteen years. It's the room where they've been waiting. The room has history. It has presence. It's not pretty — it's deep in the western corridor, it's far from the main living areas, it's a place where the light is dim and the air is quiet. But it has truth. And I think truth matters more than aesthetics in a memorial."

Elena nodded slowly. "A hall. Not a room. We clear out the storage shelves, we refurbish what needs refurbishing, we create something that looks and feels intentional. A hall where the dead are honored, not stored."

Laila's jaw tightened, just slightly. The kind of tightening that meant she was holding something back.

"What is it?" Elena asked gently. She had learned gentleness as a skill, not as a personality trait. She was not naturally gentle — she was naturally direct, naturally driven, naturally focused on outcomes over feelings. But she had learned, through fifteen years of working alongside Laila and Sana and the other emotional core of the colony, that gentleness was sometimes the most effective tool for achieving an outcome, especially when the outcome required people to do something they were not ready to do.

"Three people," Laila said. "Two of them people I knew well. One of them — Priya — someone I had dinner with three days before she died. Someone I was arguing with about reactor maintenance protocols three days before a valve failure killed her." She paused. "They shouldn't be the only ones. Not in a permanent memorial. There will be more."

The words hung in the medbay air like the words of a weather report that everyone understood but nobody wanted to hear.

"I know," Elena said. "There will be more. But we start with three. We start with the names we have. And we leave space for the names that will come, because on Mars, the names will come, and the memorial needs to accommodate them without needing to be rebuilt each time."

Laila nodded. She walked back to her desk, sat down, and looked at the inventory tablet she had been reviewing. Her eyes were on the screen but she was seeing something else — faces, names, the specific and irreplaceable way each of the dead had occupied space in the world and in her memory.

"I want to design it," she said.

Elena blinked. "The memorial?"

"The memorial. Or the hall. Whatever we call it. I want to design it. Not the engineering — I know you or Arun will handle the structural work. But the content. The names, the records, the way their lives and deaths are presented. I want— I want to control that. Because I was there. For two of them. I was in the room when— when the systems failed and the bodies stopped working and there was nothing I could do. I know what it looks like when effort is not enough. I want to make sure the memorial reflects that. Not with despair. Not with nihilism. But with the honest, unflinching recognition that effort is sometimes not enough and we try anyway."

Elena stood. She walked to Laila's desk, placed her hand on Laila's shoulder — a gesture that was, for Elena, significant, the kind of physical contact she reserved for moments when words were insufficient and the need for human connection exceeded the awkwardness of initiating it.

"I think that's the best thing you've ever told me I should do," Elena said.

Laila looked at the hand on her shoulder. She did not shrug it off. She did not acknowledge it explicitly. But she did not reject it, either, and for Laila, not rejecting something was the closest she could come to accepting it.

"Thank you," Laila said.

Elena withdrew her hand. "I'll start the engineering work. We'll need to clear Bay 22-West, which means— it means we need to move them first."

Laila's expression became the expression it became when she needed to separate the emotional content of a situation from its practical content and deal with the practical content first. "Yes. We'll need to move them. Temporarily, during refurbishment. I'll handle that. I'll be with them during the move. I won't— I won't delegate it."

"Of course," Elena said. "I wouldn't expect you to."

Elena turned to leave. At the door, she paused.

"Laila. This is important. I want you to know that I understand what you're doing. You're not just designing a room. You're deciding how this colony will remember its dead. Forever. Every child born on Mars — starting with Sana's boy — will grow up knowing the names of the people who came before them and the price they paid for a place to live. That's not a small thing. That's one of the largest things we can do."

Laila was looking at the inventory tablet. She was not reading it.

"I know," she said. "That's why it has to be right."

## SCENE THREE: THE MOVING

The transfer was scheduled for a time when the colony was quiet — the hours that were officially designated as rest time but were, in practice, the hours when the people who couldn't sleep wandered the corridors and the people who were trying to avoid thinking about things they couldn't control worked at tasks that required focus.

Laila did it alone. Not because she wanted to — solitude was not something Laila enjoyed — but because it was her responsibility, and the responsibility was one she had decided could not be shared.

She entered Storage Bay 22-West with a portable cryogenic transfer unit, a specialized piece of equipment that had been designed for exactly this scenario: the temporary transfer of cryogenically preserved remains from one containment system to another without a significant change in temperature. On Earth, it would have been handled by a team of professionals in a facility designed for this kind of work. On Mars, it was handled by one person in a storage bay at the far end of a corridor, because one person was what was available, and on Mars, available was better than ideal.

The containment units stood in a row along the eastern wall of the bay. Three of them. Each one a rectangular structure, roughly two meters long by one meter wide by one meter high, with transparent viewing panels that allowed the contents to be seen without opening the unit and compromising the internal temperature.

Laila approached the first one. Chen Wei.

Through the viewing panel, she could see the outline of a body — not in detail, because the cryogenic frost and the condensation that built up over fifteen years of operation had made the panels increasingly opaque, but enough to recognize the shape. The shape of a person. A person she had known. A person who had laughed at bad jokes in the common area and argued passionately about geological formations and who had, on his last day, spent four hours outside the habitat collecting samples that the colony was still analyzing when his body was brought to this room.

"Chen," Laila said, and her voice echoed in the small space with a quality that she found both unsettling and appropriate. "I'm going to move you."

She placed her hands on the containment unit and activated the transfer procedure. The unit hummed — a low, steady vibration that indicated the internal systems were functioning correctly, that the temperature inside was stable, that the person within was preserved in the closest possible approximation of stasis that human technology could produce.

She moved it onto the transfer platform, locked it into place, secured the straps that would keep it from shifting during transport. She repeated the process with the second unit — Olena Kovalenko, the botanist who had made the desert bloom — and with the third — Priya Sharma, the engineer who had died fixing the thing that was supposed to keep people like her safe.

Three units. Three people. On a platform that Laila pushed through the corridors of Habitat Three with the steady, unhurried pace of someone performing a duty that was simultaneously the most important and the most mundane thing she had ever done.

She did not encounter anyone. The corridors were empty, the rest-time quiet unbroken by footsteps or conversation. The ventilation system hummed. The lights were dimmed to their rest-time levels, casting long shadows that made the familiar corridors look unfamiliar, like a place she knew but was seeing through a different lens.

She took the platform to the emergency staging area — a large, climate-controlled room that was normally used for equipment testing and maintenance — and parked it. She set up a temporary monitoring system that would track the temperature of each containment unit and alert her via comm if any of them exceeded the acceptable threshold. She checked the readings. All three were within parameters. All three were stable. All three were exactly as they had been in Storage Bay 22-West, just in a different room.

Satisfied, she sat down in the chair next to the platform and waited.

She did not know what she was waiting for. Time, mostly. Time for the refurbishment of Storage Bay 22-West to begin. Time for the colony to process, in its distributed, collective way, the knowledge that their dead were being moved not toward home — home was no longer a place their dead could go — but toward remembrance.

Toward a hall.

She sat with the three containment units for forty-seven minutes. Forty-seven minutes in which she thought about Chen and his geological samples, about Olena and her plants, about Priya and the valve. Forty-seven minutes in which she sat in the presence of the dead and did not look away, which was something she had always been good at — looking at things that other people looked away from, whether they were wounds or failures or the frozen outlines of colleagues who had not made it to the end.

Arun found her there.

He had been walking through the corridors, looking for her — not because she had asked him to, but because he knew that when Laila was doing something difficult and important, she preferred to have support that was present but not interfering, the kind of support that said *I am here* without saying *you need me.*

"Laila," he said, from the doorway.

She turned. "Arun."

"How are you?"

The question was simple. The answer was complicated. Laila considered the question for a moment, then decided to answer it in the way she answered most questions: honestly, directly, without unnecessary elaboration.

"I'm doing my job," she said.

Arun nodded. He entered the room and stood beside the platform, looking at the three containment units with the same steady attention that Laila was giving them.

"They look— peaceful," he said. The word surprised him, and he corrected himself. "No, that's wrong. They don't look peaceful. They look— I don't know. They look like they're waiting."

"They are waiting," Laila said. "Not for a return ship, not for resurrection, not for any of the things that science fiction has told us to expect. They're waiting for a decision. For the living to decide what happens to them. For us to decide what their deaths mean."

Arun absorbed this. He was a man who thought in systems and solutions, but he had learned, over fifteen years of living on Mars, that not everything was a system and not everything had a solution. Some things just had to be endured, and endurance was its own kind of solution.

"The hall," he said. "Are you going to design it?"

"Yes."

"What will it—" He stopped. Reconsidered. Asked a different question. "What will it look like?"

Laila thought about this. She had been thinking about it since she spoke with Elena, and the thinking had produced a clear image in her mind, an image she had not yet shared with anyone because it was still forming and because the things that mattered most to her were the things she was most careful about.

"It will be the room as it is," she said. "Not as it was. Not refurbished beyond recognition. The room is what it is — a room in the far corridor, dim, quiet, with concrete walls and a metal floor and a ventilation system that whispers instead of hums. We won't make it beautiful. We'll make it honest."

"Honest."

"Yes. Chen didn't die in a chapel. Olena didn't die in a garden. Priya didn't die in a ceremony. They died in the same place we all might die — while working, while trying, while doing the things that needed to be done in a colony that doesn't stop because someone has died. The hall should reflect that. Not with flowers or candles or the kind of decoration we'd use on Earth. With records. With data. With the specifics of each person's life and death. The date. The cause. The contribution. The name, in the language they spoke at home. The thing they wanted most to do on Mars and the thing they did instead. Everything."

Arun was quiet. Then: "That sounds— hard."

"It is."

"Are you ready?"

Laila looked at the three containment units. She looked at Arun. She looked at the ceiling of the emergency staging area, past it, through it, toward the corridors and the rooms and the people who were, at this moment, sleeping or working or thinking or trying not to think.

"I'm not ready," she said. "But I'm the person who has to do it, and I believe that, in the end, doing is more important than being ready."

Arun sat down beside her. They sat together in the quiet room, in the presence of the three who had not made it to fifteen years, and they sat until the colony's dawn cycle began and the lights brightened and the rest time ended and the day began again.

Three containment units. One doctor. One engineer. Forty-seven minutes of sitting with the dead.

It was not much, by the standards of ceremony. But it was honest. And Laila had decided that, on Mars, honesty was the only ceremony that mattered.

## SCENE FOUR: THE NAMING

The design process took three weeks.

Three weeks in which Laila balanced her medical duties with the work of creating a memorial, splitting her time between patients who were alive and the three who were not, between the urgent needs of the living and the quiet, patient needs of the dead. She conducted her medical rounds in the medbay, attended to injuries and illnesses and the routine maintenance of two hundred human bodies, and then, when the rounds were done and the patients were stable and the colony was resting, she went to the staging area and sat with the containment units and thought about what a hall should contain.

She visited Elena's quarters with a list of requirements. Not a design brief — Laila did not use design briefs, and Elena did not respond well to them anyway. A list, handwritten on a recycled supply tablet because Laila preferred paper — or its digital equivalent — for things that mattered.

EFFECTS FOR MEMORIAL HALL — STORAGE BAY 22-WEST:

1. No decorative elements. The room is what it is. Cleaned, repaired, illuminated, but not beautified. Beauty implies intention to please. The hall should not try to please. It should try to tell the truth.

2. Names on the walls. Not plaques — the colony doesn't have materials for plaques, and anyway, plaques imply permanence that we cannot guarantee. Names written directly on the wall. Painted or engraved. In the language the person spoke at home. Chen will have his name in Chinese characters. Olena will have hers in Ukrainian. Priya will have hers in both Hindi and English.

3. Biographical data for each person. Date of birth. Date of arrival on Mars. Date of death. Cause of death. Primary role in the colony. Most significant contribution. Personal quote — something they said, or something that was said about them, something that captures the person rather than the death. (I have collected quotes for Chen and Olena. Need one for Priya. I'll ask Tariq.)

4. Cause of death to be stated plainly. No euphemisms. Chen died due to a pressure seal failure during EVA. Olena died due to a pulmonary embolism. Priya died due to a valve failure during reactor maintenance. The facts are sufficient. They do not need softening.

5. A record of every living person who was in the colony at the time of each death. Because death on Mars is not an individual event. It is a communal event. Everyone who was here when Chen died was changed by it. Everyone who was here when Olena died was changed by it. Everyone who was here when Priya died was changed by it. The record should reflect that.

6. Space for future names. Twelve empty positions, minimum. I say twelve because— I don't want to be more specific than that. Twelve is enough for the immediate future. If we need more, we'll expand.

7. A single bench. Not a comfortable bench. A simple one. Metal. Sturdy. For sitting and remembering.

8. Lighting. Dim, but sufficient to read the walls. A single overhead light, adjustable. No ambiance lighting. No mood-setting. Just light enough to see the names.

9. The containment units will be removed permanently. I will oversee the— the transition. I have determined that, for each person, the most respectful course is— I'll write this separately. It's not for you to read. It's for me to do.

10. A door with a sign. Not "Storage Bay 22-West." Something else. Something that tells people what this room is before they enter it. I have a candidate but need to discuss it.

Elena read the list. Twice. Then she looked at Laila.

"This is the most detailed thing you've ever written," Elena said.

"It's the most important thing I've ever written," Laila replied.

Elena nodded. "The engineering is straightforward. Structural cleaning, wall repair, new lighting, the bench — all manageable. I'll start tomorrow."

"Thank you."

"Laila." Elena paused. "What about the sign. What's your candidate?"

Laila thought about this. She had been thinking about it for three weeks, through medical rounds and supply inventories and late nights sitting with the containment units, through the birth of Sana's baby and the activation of NO FLEET COMING and every decision and disappointment and small victory that had characterized the colony's existence since the fire.

"HALL OF THE DEAD," she said.

Elena was quiet. She let the words sit in the room between them, absorbing their weight, considering their meaning, testing them against every other possibility she had been carrying in the back of her mind.

"Hall of the Dead," she repeated.

"It's direct. No euphemisms. No metaphors. No attempt to soften what it is for what people who died in this colony. It's what it is. A hall. That honors the dead."

Elena considered this. She considered alternatives — MEMORIAL HALL, REMEMBRANCE CHAPEL, THE GONE — and found each one wanting. MEMORIAL HALL was too generic. REMEMBRANCE CHAPEL was too religious, too Earth-centric, too soft. THE GONE was too poetic, too vague, too willing to let the specifics of loss dissolve into the abstraction of absence.

"Hall of the Dead," Elena said finally. "It's honest. And the room needs to be honest."

Laila nodded. For her, this was confirmation. Not validation — she did not need validation, she had already decided — but confirmation that she was communicating clearly and that her clarity was being received by someone who understood what it meant to build something honest in a world that often rewarded dishonesty.

"I'll draft the engineering specs," Elena said. "We'll start the work in two days. That gives you time to— finalize the other things. The quotes, the records, the transition."

"Two days is sufficient," Laila said. "I've already collected what I need for Chen and Olena. I just need Priya's quote, and I know who to ask."

She did. She knew exactly who. And she knew that the conversation she was about to have would be one of the most difficult conversations of her fifteen-year career on Mars.

Which, considering that her fifteen-year career on Mars had included delivering babies in burning buildings and losing patients despite doing everything she could and sitting with the dead in empty rooms, was saying something.

## SCENE FIVE: THE QUOTE

She found Tariq in the reactor maintenance bay, where he had been spending most of his time since Priya's death — not because he had to, Elena had reassigned his reactor duties to another engineer out of consideration, but because Tariq himself had requested the work and Elena had, after a brief internal debate, decided that work was sometimes the best form of therapy.

Tariq was wearing his reactor suit, the heavy, insulated garment that protected technicians from the radiation and heat of the power system, and he was knee-deep in a diagnostic of Cooling Loop Three, the same system that Priya had been working on when the valve had failed.

"Laila," he said, standing as she approached. "Is everything all right? Is Sana—?"

"Sana is fine," Laila said quickly. "The baby is fine. Everything is fine." She paused. "I need to talk to you about Priya."

Tariq's face changed. Not dramatically — he was a man who had learned to control his face, the way people on Mars learned to control everything that could be controlled — but enough. His eyes lost a fraction of their warmth. His jaw set. His hands, freed from the diagnostic tools he had been holding, went to his sides and stayed there.

"What do you need?" he asked, his voice carefully neutral.

Laila stood beside him in the reactor bay. The hum of the power system was a constant presence in the background, a reminder of the energy that kept the colony alive, of the thing that Priya had died maintaining, of the fact that the same system that killed her was the same system that kept her son alive.

"We're building a memorial," Laila said. "In Storage Bay 22-West. For Chen, Olena, and Priya. And — eventually — for everyone else who dies here. I'm designing it. I need a quote for Priya. Something she said. Something that she was. I have quotes for Chen and Olena. I don't have one for her. I thought you might."

Tariq was looking at the diagnostic panel. He was not reading it. His eyes were on the screen but his mind was somewhere else — somewhere in the past, somewhere in the three days before the valve failure, somewhere in the space between grief and acceptance that he had been occupying for eighteen months and that showed no signs of closing.

"She had a— a way of talking about the reactor," he said slowly, finding the words the way people find words when they are trying to articulate something that has been sitting in the dark for a long time. "She called it— she called it the heart. Not metaphorically. Practically. She said: 'If you think of the habitat as a body, the reactor is the heart. It pumps energy to everything. When the heart stops, everything stops. So you don't just maintain the heart. You listen to it.'"

He paused. His hand reached out and touched the cooling loop diagnostic panel — the same panel he touched every day, a gesture that had become habitual, almost ritual, the way people touch the things that connect them to the people they have lost.

"She used to tell me," he continued, his voice gaining strength as the memory became less painful and more precious, "that the reactor had a rhythm. A sound. She said: 'Close your eyes and stand in the reactor bay and listen. You can hear the cooling pumps. You can hear the turbines. You can hear the flow of energy through the system. It has a rhythm. And if the rhythm changes, something is wrong. So you don't just check the gauges. You listen to the heart. Because the heart will tell you what the gauges won't — it will tell you when it's afraid.'"

Tariq turned to face Laila. His eyes were bright, but he did not cry. He was past the point of crying, or had found a place beyond it, or had simply decided that crying was a luxury that a father could not afford.

"'You don't just maintain the heart,'" he repeated. "'You listen to it.' That was her. That's what I want on the wall. Not a poem. Not something from a book on Earth. Something she said. Something specific. Something that tells whoever reads it who she was and what she believed."

Laila recorded the quote on her tablet. She did not embellish it. She did not edit it. She reproduced it exactly as Tariq had spoken it, with all its repetitions and pauses and hesitations, because those were the features of the quote that made it real, and reality was what the hall needed.

"Thank you," she said.

"Thank you," Tariq replied. "For doing this. For remembering her. For— for making sure that the people who come after us will know that she was here and that she mattered."

"She was here," Laila said. "And she mattered."

She left the reactor bay. The walk back to her quarters was the same walk she had made a thousand times — the same corridors, the same lights, the same ventilation system humming in the background — but it felt different, because walks feel different when you are carrying something heavy, and Laila was carrying a quote from a dead engineer to her son and the weight of all three names on the walls of a room that would soon become a hall.

She reached her quarters. She set up her desk. She finalized the memorial records for Chen, Olena, and Priya. She wrote their quotes in their languages — Chen's in Chinese, Olena's in Ukrainian, Priya's in Hindi and English. She reviewed the biographical data. She confirmed the dates, the causes, the contributions. She assembled the records in a format that could be mounted on the walls of the refurbished bay.

It took her the entire night. When dawn came, the colony's artificial dawn that brightened the corridors and signaled the start of a day that was, like every day on Mars, a negotiation between survival and meaning, Laila was still at her desk, reviewing the final record for the third time.

Three names. Three stories. Three deaths and the lives that preceded them.

It was not much, by the standards of the dead on Earth, where billions had lived and died and the memorials to the departed covered continents and filled cities and required the kind of space that Mars, in all her vast red emptiness, could not provide.

But it was enough. Because on Mars, everything was measured differently. Everything was scaled to the size of what two hundred people could build and maintain and meaningfully honor. Everything was intimate — the birth, the death, the memorial, the child sleeping in a mother's arms three corridors away from the room where the dead were waiting to be remembered.

Laila saved the files. She sent them to Elena. She turned off her desk light. She lay down on her bed, closed her eyes, and, for the first time in three weeks, slept.

## SCENE SIX: THE OPENING

The hall opened on Sol 5,530.

Elena had worked for two weeks alongside a team of volunteers — not assigned, not ordered, but volunteered, because the request had gone out through the colony's informal communication network and the response had been immediate and unanimous. People wanted to help. Not because they had to, because on Mars you did what you had to, but because this was different. This was not maintenance or repair or the kind of labor that kept the lights on. This was the labor of memory. And the labor of memory was something that people chose freely.

The room was cleaned. The walls were repaired. The scorched marks from the fire that had once been present in this part of the corridor were removed, not because they needed removing but because the room was being repurposed and repurposing required a clean start. The lighting was installed — a single overhead fixture, dim and adjustable, capable of illuminating the walls without creating an atmosphere of artificial comfort. The bench was built by Arun, who had insisted on making it himself because Priya had been his colleague and he wanted the bench — the one piece of furniture in a room full of standing names — to be something he could be proud of.

And the names were painted on the walls by Laila, who had, despite her lack of artistic training, created lettering that was clean, precise, and unembellished — the kind of lettering that did not try to be beautiful but was beautiful because of its honesty, its directness, its refusal to add anything that was not necessary.
